# Story plan — The Portal That Nobody Made

> This is an unlocked Story proposal. It develops the current direction without recording a creative lock or claiming production validation.

## Development status

The film is designed as a self-contained mystery of approximately 20 minutes. Its plot follows one personal journey through a single, self-consistent history: the protagonist discovers a portal, sees the aftermath of a disaster, travels to a point before his discovery, becomes the portal’s builder, and then lives through the disaster whose incomplete aftermath frightened him.

The working destruction mechanism is a short chain of lava ignition, temporary spruce staging and connected timber supports. It is narratively integrated but remains provisional until its range, timing, fire spread and water response are reproduced in the intended Minecraft version.

## Audience promise

A lone player in a private survival world finds a lit portal that nobody else could have made. Entering it reveals different moments of the same ravine rather than the Nether. The intended pleasure is the gradual conversion of spatial details, construction habits and apparent threats into one readable causal pattern. The mystery resolves through actions shown from opposite sides, while the climax asks whether a meaningful choice remains when an observed outcome cannot be replaced.

The story would disappoint if the portal led to an ordinary adventure, if history were protected by an invisible force, if the narrator knowingly lied, if the wolf survived through an unprepared convenience, or if the fire depended on an arbitrary supernatural event.

## Story in chronological order

1. The protagonist builds a modest timber-and-stone homestead on the west rim of a ravine, tames a wolf and establishes a descending wooden maintenance stair. A contained lava shelf lies below the stair, while an eastern stone drain offers a non-flammable route away from the house. He routinely leaves the wolf seated when mining.
2. Roughly twenty minutes before the discovery seen in the opening, the protagonist’s older travelling self is ejected into the portal cave. The frame does not yet exist. From concealment he sees his younger self and the wolf above, proving that he has reached his own recent past.
3. The older self wants to warn the younger without making him avoid the portal. He takes three red wool blocks from an outdoor supply barrel and begins a route marker from the wolf pen towards the eastern drain. The younger self approaches before an arrowhead can be completed, so the older self hides. This is the unexplained strip the younger self later dismisses as an abandoned marker.
4. The older self recognises the cave’s odd left-wall torch position and asymmetrical footing as details from the portal he entered. He decides to reproduce them. He mines local obsidian from the lava shelf, cools one irregular cobblestone block at the frame’s base and uses a short length of spruce staging to reach the final frame blocks. The staging closes the safe gap between the lava shelf and the existing timber stair. He lights the completed portal and hides.
5. At dusk, the younger self finishes his chores, leaves the wolf sitting and descends. He notices the incomplete red wool line, the reversed torch and the cobblestone footing, but none is decisive alone. He finds the impossible portal and chooses to enter. The older self watches without warning him because he believes the journey supplies the only foreknowledge capable of saving anything.
6. The younger self arrives at dawn after the homestead has burned. The geography is unchanged, the wolf pen is empty and a lone figure crosses the eastern ridge. The figure performs the protagonist’s habitual two-crouch orientation check and places a torch on the left-facing wall, but distance prevents identification. The younger self chases, loses the figure and returns to the portal.
7. Crossing again ejects the younger self into the pre-discovery cave described above. He becomes the older travelling self who leaves the marker, mines the obsidian and builds the portal. No material is created by the loop: the wool, obsidian and timber all come from local resources with ordinary origins. Only the remembered arrangement of the portal lacks an external first design.
8. After the younger self enters, the older self notices smoke. The proposed Minecraft chain is that the nearby lava ignites his temporary spruce staging, which carries fire to the connected maintenance stair and then to separated fronts beneath the timber house. He breaks burning stair blocks and moves his single water source across the roof, but the spread is already too distributed to preserve the structure.
9. The seated wolf is trapped behind its pen while the exposed yard burns. The protagonist hears it as part of the roof gives way. He stops moving the water from block to block in defence of the house. Instead, he relocates the source to the eastern stone drain, creating a temporary wet approach, reaches the pen, opens it and releases the wolf from its seated state. The wolf follows him through the prepared route while the house continues to burn.
10. At dawn the ruin matches the future image exactly. When the portal flares, the older self understands that his earlier travelling self is arriving. He keeps the wolf below the ridge line, deliberately crosses the visible crest, repeats the two-crouch check and places the left-wall torch. His earlier self sees the silhouette and is drawn back towards the portal. Once that self has crossed into the past, the older self extinguishes the frame. He then leads the wolf away at first light.

## Plot and causality

The active opposition is an information conflict between versions of the same person, intensified by physical time pressure. The younger self wants an explanation and a chance to prevent the ruin. The older self wants to preserve the journey because it produced the knowledge required for the rescue. Neither is controlled by the timeline: the older self repeatedly chooses concealment, incomplete warning and reconstruction because he fears that direct contact would remove the only path he knows can save the wolf.

The main chain is causal rather than coincidental:

- Exclusive authorship makes the portal an intolerable contradiction, so curiosity causes entry.
- Entry reveals the burned home and absent wolf, so apparent total loss causes a second crossing.
- The frame’s absence and the visible younger self prove that the second destination is the past.
- The incomplete marker becomes something the protagonist remembers seeing, proving that intervention can be part of established history.
- That proof, plus his desire to give his younger self foreknowledge, causes him to build the portal voluntarily.
- His hurried construction creates the proposed flammable connection that causes the fire.
- His first attempt to save the building consumes the time and water needed elsewhere, forcing a value choice.
- Redirecting the water and releasing the wolf makes the apparently empty future compatible with survival.
- Concealing the wolf and recreating the silhouette causes his earlier self to complete the journey, closing the information loop.

Removing the portal entry removes the investigation, construction and rescue knowledge. Removing the red marker removes the protagonist’s first proof that his interventions already belong to history. Removing the construction hazard makes the disaster arbitrary. Removing the wolf choice leaves the fixed timeline emotionally inert. Removing the final silhouette breaks the fair identity reveal and the cause of the second crossing.

## Audience presentation

The film follows the protagonist’s personal order rather than world chronology.

- The opening establishes the private world, the wolf, the red wool strip, the timber stair, the lava glow and the protagonist’s confidence in his own authorship.
- The portal scene makes its builder the primary question. Its footing and reversed torch are visible but not uniquely identifying.
- The aftermath confirms matching geography before explaining time. The empty pen supports fear without proving death. The distant figure supports another-player and future-self interpretations.
- The pre-discovery arrival rules out a parallel copy. When the protagonist lays the wool blocks he remembers, the audience can infer a fixed history before he accepts it.
- Mining and construction answer who built the portal through matched physical actions. The reveal precedes the climax so that the ending can resolve value rather than merely information.
- The fire exposes the ordinary cause and reproduces the damage already shown. No second outcome is presented.
- The reverse view of the ridge reveals the hidden wolf and confirms the silhouette’s identity. Earlier images remain true; their meaning changes.

Narration stays with what the protagonist believed at each point. It may say that he thought the wolf was gone or believed he could still prevent the fire. It must not state that the wolf died, pretend not to recognise an action after recognition, or imply that several versions of the disaster occurred.

## Characters and relationships

### The protagonist

He wants to identify the portal’s builder and prevent the destruction of the home he authored. He needs to separate preserving a structure from caring for what made it a home. He fears helplessness and interprets careful observation as a route to control. His practical strategy is to compare persistent blocks, leave markers, reproduce the portal and prepare against the fire. His contradiction is that curiosity begins the journey while caution later makes him conceal decisive information. His limitation is not lack of intelligence but his tendency to protect a complete plan after its purpose has changed. His boundary is tested when the wolf and house cannot both receive his remaining time; he refuses to sacrifice the living companion for recoverable blocks.

His consequential choices are to enter, cross again, avoid confronting his younger self, leave an incomplete warning, build the portal, let his younger self enter, abandon the roof, rescue the wolf, recreate the silhouette and finally extinguish the portal.

### The wolf

The wolf is a companion rather than a symbolic prop. Ordinary routines establish trust before danger: it follows during chores, waits at the pen and responds when released from sitting. It cannot understand the marker, open the gate or choose a safe temporal strategy. Its vulnerability turns an abstract question about causality into a concrete responsibility.

The relationship begins with the protagonist treating the wolf as one secure element within an owned home. It ends with him accepting responsibility for the wolf even after the owned structure is lost. The wolf’s absence from the first aftermath is a limitation of the protagonist’s viewpoint, not evidence of death.

## Movement of the story

| Movement | Temporary goal and strategy | Complication and reversal | Outcome and changed state |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. The authored world | Finish dusk chores, verify the cave and identify the impossible builder | Familiar marker and torch placements are slightly wrong; the portal contradicts single-player authorship | He enters by choice; security becomes temporal displacement |
| 2. Ashes before cause | Find the wolf and catch the apparent survivor in the ruined homestead | The pen is empty, the figure evades him and the portal is his only route away | He crosses again seeking correction; pursuit becomes entrapment in the past |
| 3. The wrong side of yesterday | Warn the younger self without preventing the journey | His incomplete wool route is the marker he already remembers, so intervention is not a new outcome | He accepts that he is participating in history and chooses to become the builder |
| 4. Becoming the cause | Build the remembered portal before the younger self arrives | Local obsidian solves the material problem, but hurried spruce staging connects lava to the timber stair | The mystery is answered; the rescue opportunity and destructive cause are created together |
| 5. What can still be saved | Prevent the known fire, then preserve what remains meaningful | One water source cannot cover separated fronts; the trapped wolf makes delay consequential | He redirects the water, saves the wolf, recreates the silhouette and closes the portal |

## Scene progression

| Scene | Entry and objective | Conflict or visual value | Turn and outcome | Exit state | Production need |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Dusk routine | Secure homestead; finish chores and descend | Wolf bond, incomplete red wool line, timber stair above lava | Purple light appears below; he investigates | Calm authorship becomes unease | Intact homestead, seated wolf, reusable geography shot |
| 2. Nobody’s portal | Identify the builder without entering | Frame, asymmetrical footing and reversed torch contradict his memory | Curiosity defeats caution; he enters | Displaced from the known present | Portal hero set and controlled transition |
| 3. Burned morning | Locate home and wolf | Same ravine, missing blocks, ash, empty pen | A distant player-shaped figure appears | Loss gains a possible culprit | Burned-state reset and matched camera positions |
| 4. The ridge figure | Catch the figure or find a route back | Signature crouch-and-torch action; wolf remains below sight line | Figure vanishes; he crosses the portal again | He expects another attempt | Distant duplicate silhouette only |
| 5. Cave before the frame | Determine where and when he is | Bare portal wall and undamaged landmarks | He sees his younger self and wolf above | The destination becomes his own past | Empty cave state and restrained double blocking |
| 6. The warning he remembers | Move or warn the wolf without being seen | Younger self’s proximity and fear of stopping the journey | He abandons the unfinished wool arrow | He knows his actions formed remembered history | Exterior barrel, three wool blocks, sight-line concealment |
| 7. The builder’s obligation | Find a route that preserves a rescue chance | No exit frame, limited time and local resource requirement | He recognises that he must construct the portal | Investigation becomes commitment | Close matching of opening clues |
| 8. Construction | Finish the frame before the younger self descends | Obsidian mining beside lava requires hurried staging | The lit frame exactly matches the opening | Answer achieved; latent fire created | Mining montage, water/lava continuity, testable staging geometry |
| 9. Opposite side of the opening | Let the younger self enter without revealing him | He can still call out or dismantle the frame | He remains silent; smoke appears after entry | Preserved loop becomes immediate danger | Controlled two-avatar angles or eyeline substitutes |
| 10. Losing the house | Stop fire spreading through the supports | Separated fronts, limited water and his own staging as origin | A collapse exposes the trapped wolf’s cry | Saving both is no longer credible | Verified fire rig and replaceable burn stages |
| 11. The choice | Reach and release the wolf | Burning yard and the water source currently defending blocks | He moves the water to the stone drain and abandons the roof | Wolf follows; house remains doomed | Reliable wolf blocking and water-route rehearsal |
| 12. The other side of the silhouette | Leave without disrupting what his earlier self saw | The arriving self must see enough to pursue but not the wolf | He recreates the ridge action, waits for the crossing and douses the portal | Mystery closed; relationship preserved | One controlled overlap, reverse angle and dawn final plate |

## Setups, payoffs, and continuity

| Setup | Initial reading | Pay-off |
|---|---|---|
| Private single-player authorship | The portal implies an intruder or anomaly | The protagonist physically builds it from local materials |
| Asymmetrical cobblestone footing | An unknown builder’s signature | Water used during hurried obsidian mining creates it |
| Reversed cave torch | Someone navigates differently | The same protagonist places it while approaching from the other temporal direction |
| Three red wool blocks without an arrowhead | Abandoned decoration or old marker | He lays them as an interrupted warning; the route later guides his rescue |
| Timber stair separated from a lava shelf | Background survival geography | Temporary staging closes the gap and permits ordinary fire spread |
| One movable water source | Routine equipment | He must choose whether its next placement protects blocks or opens a route to the wolf |
| Seated wolf and closed pen | Safe domestic routine | The wolf cannot self-evacuate; the protagonist must reach and release it |
| Empty future pen | The wolf may have died | The final reverse angle shows it alive below the ridge |
| Ridge figure’s two crouches and left-wall torch | A knowledgeable stranger | The protagonist deliberately repeats the action at the end |
| Identical burned composition | Foreknowledge might create a better version | The same ruin remains, but its apparent total loss was an incomplete reading |

Continuity must preserve the west-rim homestead, north-wall portal cave, lava shelf, connected timber stair, eastern stone drain and ridge sight line across all states. Portal obsidian, red wool and staging timber have ordinary local origins. The protagonist’s equipment may coexist with its younger state during temporal overlap, but no item may be introduced without an earlier source. The wolf is never shown dead, injured beyond recovery or visible during the first ridge silhouette.

## Ending and meaning

The climax grows from the protagonist’s earlier decisions rather than from the timeline correcting him. He chose the risky construction, chose silence when he could warn his younger self, and initially chose to spend scarce time defending the building. The fire converts those choices into immediate pressure. His decisive action is not accepting passivity: it is reallocating the only useful resource and his remaining time towards the wolf.

The final ruin is unchanged, satisfying the established single-history rule. Its emotional meaning changes because the first visit showed an empty frame, not a complete account. The closing image reverses the opening: instead of leaving the wolf seated beside an intact home while descending alone, the protagonist walks away from the burned home with the wolf following, and the unlit portal stands behind them.

A provisional thematic argument is that agency does not require every fact to be rewritable. A person may be unable to preserve the form of a life yet still choose which responsibility carries forwards. The unexplained origin of the portal’s temporal routing can remain open as a question of authorship, provided it is not used to conceal any cause required for the fire, rescue or identity reveal.

## Evidence and scope still required

Before Story lock, production testing must confirm a deterministic version-specific layout for lava ignition, fire spread, water placement and wolf pathing. If the proposed staging chain cannot be reproduced reliably, its geometry should change while preserving the causal function: the protagonist’s hurried portal construction must create an ordinary, visible hazard that his later value choice cannot erase. No audience test, animatic validation or capture validation is claimed at this stage.

# Continuity bible — The Portal That Nobody Made

## Canon authority

- Canon owner: Luan
- Current canon version: Story proposal 0.1 — unlocked, 15 July 2026
- Locked upstream artefacts: None stated. The supplied Direction is explicitly unlocked.
- Rule for proposed canon changes: record the proposal, dependency impact, and human decision before altering locked work.
- Status of this bible: proposed continuity for human review; it does not record a story lock or production validation.

## Timeline

### World chronology

| World time | Objective event |
|---|---|
| W0 — established past | The protagonist builds the west-rim homestead, timber maintenance stair, wolf pen and eastern stone drain. He tames the wolf and crafts or acquires his ordinary tools and water bucket. A safe air-and-stone gap separates the lower lava shelf from the timber stair. |
| W1 — shortly before discovery | The travelling protagonist arrives through a transient portal plane at the bare north-wall cave. His younger self is still above. He takes three red wool blocks from the local exterior barrel, lays an incomplete evacuation route, places the reversed cave torch, mines local obsidian and erects the portal. His temporary spruce staging closes the gap between lava and timber. |
| W2 — dusk discovery | The younger protagonist completes chores, seats the wolf, notices the red strip, finds the portal and enters. The older protagonist watches from concealment and chooses silence. |
| W3 — night fire | The proposed ordinary ignition chain carries fire from lava to staging, stair and house. The older protagonist first defends the structure, then redirects water through the eastern drain and releases the wolf. The house burns to the state already observed. |
| W4 — dawn aftermath | The older protagonist and wolf travel below the eastern ridge. The younger travelling protagonist arrives from W2, sees the ruin and glimpses the older silhouette. The older self deliberately recreates the crouch-and-torch clue. The younger self crosses from W4 to W1. After that transit, the older self extinguishes the portal and continues forwards with the wolf. |

### Protagonist’s personal order

P1 W2 discovery → P2 W4 aftermath and silhouette → P3 W1 pre-frame ejection → P4 W1 warning and construction → P5 W2 observation of his own entry → P6 W3 fire and rescue → P7 W4 recreation of the silhouette and departure.

Every event occurs once in world history. Apparent repetition is a later personal version observing or causing an event that an earlier personal version has already witnessed.

### Closed causal information

The protagonist builds the portal because he remembers entering that arrangement. The physical matter is not bootstrapped: obsidian is mined at W1, wool comes from the W1 barrel and spruce comes from local stock. The first external origin of the copied temporal arrangement is intentionally open in this proposal. It must not be extended into an explanation that changes the established route without human approval.

## Relationships and power balance

The protagonist initially has practical power over the wolf: he commands sitting and following, controls the gate and chooses routes. This routine protects the wolf under normal conditions but creates its fire vulnerability. During the climax, that vulnerability gains decision-making power because the protagonist cannot continue treating the house as his only objective.

The relationship changes from ownership inside a controlled space to responsibility carried beyond that space. The final following state must be earned by the release action in SC-11, not by placing the wolf safely in the final shot without showing the causal link.

The protagonist’s opposition with his younger self is intrapersonal but physically staged. The older self knows more about consequences and controls concealment; the younger self controls whether the journey begins. Neither version attacks or coerces the other. The older version influences him through the portal, marker and silhouette.

## Locations, geography, travel, and blocking

### Fixed layout

- The compact timber-and-stone homestead occupies the west rim of the ravine.
- The wolf pen sits on the eastern side of the homestead beside an exposed yard.
- A stone drain or maintenance channel runs from that yard towards a lower eastern escape path. It is non-flammable and visually readable in intact and burned states.
- The timber maintenance stair descends from the west-rim undercroft towards the north-wall portal cave.
- A contained lava shelf lies below the stair. Before W1, a visible air-and-stone gap prevents a continuous flammable route to the stair.
- The portal site is a recessed cave on the north wall, visible from a controlled overlook but not directly from the house.
- The eastern ridge has an upper crest visible from the burned homestead and a lower path that conceals the wolf.

### Travel and blocking rules

- Normal movement from house to portal should feel under one minute; precise capture timing remains a production design decision.
- At W1, the younger self’s route and sight line prevent the older self from reaching the wolf without risking discovery.
- The three wool blocks point from the pen towards the stone drain but lack an arrowhead, permitting dismissal in SC-01.
- SC-04 and SC-12 use the same ridge camera line. The older protagonist is visible on the crest; the wolf remains below its occluding edge.
- Burn damage may remove timber and contents but may not change the ravine profile, portal cave, stone drain or ridge silhouette needed for recognition.

## Inventory, resources, injuries, abilities, and constraints

- Portal frame: locally mined W1 obsidian, enough for the chosen valid frame. No obsidian is taken from the future frame and carried into its own construction.
- Cobblestone footing: locally formed or mined during W1 water-and-lava work; exact geometry must be tested.
- Reversed torch: placed at W1 and still present at W2. The W4 ridge torch is a separate ordinary torch used as a repeated behavioural signature.
- Red wool: three blocks taken from the W1 exterior barrel. The incomplete marker remains through W2 and may be partly lost only during the W3 fire after its rescue-route function is established.
- Spruce staging: local W1 stock. It must visibly close the previously safe gap without making the protagonist’s mistake incomprehensible.
- Water: one carried source used for obsidian work, structural defence, rescue routing and final dousing. Capture tests must show when it is retrieved and moved.
- Tools: diamond pick for obsidian, axe for timber or gate access, flint and steel for portal ignition. Each has an ordinary pre-story origin.
- Armour: equipment condition can help distinguish silhouettes, but no durability break, injury or custom texture may carry an essential clue unless separately established and reproducible.
- Wolf: no fatal injury, unexplained healing or off-screen teleportation. Its escape depends on the SC-11 release and route.
- Time pressure: created by the younger self’s approach, visible fire spread and route closure. It must not be asserted only through narration.

Temporary coexistence between younger and older states of carried equipment is allowed as a consequence of the traveller’s worldline. It does not supply the origin of any construction material.

## Factions, history, public beliefs, and hidden truths

There are no factions, other human players, time authorities or public mythology. The world is private and solitary.

The protagonist’s initial beliefs are that he authored all persistent changes, portals lead to the expected Minecraft destination and foreknowledge should permit a corrected attempt. The hidden truths are that he built the portal, his interventions formed remembered history, his staging caused the fire, the ridge figure is his later self and the wolf survived outside the first viewpoint.

No hidden cosmic actor may be added to force self-consistency. Any later explanation of the anomaly requires a proposed canon change and dependency review.

## Recurring objects, symbols, warnings, lies, and visual motifs

- Portal plane: boundary, curiosity and self-authorship. It changes from unexplained light to deliberately built route to extinguished frame.
- Red wool line: incomplete communication. It begins as discarded visual noise, becomes proof of self-participation and finally functions as a rescue guide.
- Left-wall torch: perspective-dependent habit. It links reverse approaches and the ridge identity without dialogue.
- Two crouches: a compact avatar signature repeated exactly in SC-04 and SC-12.
- Water: first a control tool spread too thin, then a concentrated act of care.
- Timber and stone: recoverable authored form versus durable route and relationship.
- Empty frames: the portal frame and wolf pen both invite false conclusions from absence; later action supplies context.
- Opening/closing movement: the protagonist first walks away from a seated wolf towards the portal; he finally walks away from the portal with the wolf following.

There are no narrator lies. Misinterpretations must be phrased as belief, fear or incomplete observation.

- SP-01 through SP-10 have planned resolutions within this film.

## Prohibited contradictions

- Do not introduce branches, resets, alternative outcomes or repeated versions of the fire.
- Do not show the portal in the W1 cave before the protagonist constructs it; only the transient arrival plane may appear.
- Do not source portal obsidian by dismantling the future portal or otherwise create matter without an ordinary origin.
- Do not allow the red wool marker to be complete in SC-01 or absent before SC-06 in world chronology.
- Do not place the wolf in the SC-04 ridge sight line, state that it died, or use remains as false evidence.
- Do not let the wolf escape before the protagonist releases it in SC-11.
- Do not attribute the fire to temporal energy, an unseen villain or arbitrary explosion.
- Do not show timber already connecting the lava shelf to the stair before the W1 staging is added.
- Do not let one water placement visibly cover every fire front and then claim the house cannot be saved.
- Do not reveal the older self directly to the younger self before the ridge silhouette has served its causal function.
- Do not extinguish the W4 portal before the younger travelling self completes the W4-to-W1 transit.
- Do not alter the final burn pattern from the composition shown in SC-03.
- Do not treat the portal’s unexplained temporal origin as permission to change any established rule without review.
- Do not claim the candidate fire chain, wolf route or duplicate capture has been validated until evidence exists.
